lessons.title: Preparing to grade sorghum
lessons.html:
Why we grade sorghum

Grading means checking a sample of sorghum and giving it a grade according to the official grading regulations made under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990. The grade tells the buyer and the seller what the quality is, and it decides the price. A wrong grade costs the farmer or the silo money, and can lead to disputes. As a grader you must be accurate, honest and follow the method exactly.

Preparing for grading

  1. Make sure you have the current grading regulations and grade tables for sorghum. The limits for each grade come from these tables, not from memory.
  2. Check your equipment: approved moisture meter (calibrated and checked), balance or scale (level, zeroed, checked with test weights), the prescribed sieves (clean, undamaged), sample divider, sorting tray, tweezers, containers and worksheets.
  3. Clean the work area so there is no grain or dust left from the previous sample.
  4. Wear a dust coat or overalls and a dust mask. Wash hands after grading, especially if grain may be treated or mouldy.

Taking and preparing the sample

  • Take the sample from the load at several points and depths with a probe, or from the automatic sampler, following the site procedure.
  • Mix the sample well and reduce it with the approved divider to the working sample size the procedure requires. Never pick a handful from the top.
  • Label the sample with the delivery or load number, date, time and your name.

Sorghum classes

Sorghum is divided into classes, mainly by tannin content. Low-tannin sorghum is used for malt and food; high-tannin sorghum has a bitter taste and is used differently. The regulations set a test for condensed tannins. Make sure the class is correct before grading, because mixing classes lowers the value.

lessons.title: Moisture and non-compliant material
lessons.html:
Determining moisture content

Moisture content is the percentage of water in the sorghum. Grain that is too wet heats, goes mouldy and can be spoiled by insects. The regulations and the buyer set a maximum moisture level; check the current limit.

  1. Check that the moisture meter is set for sorghum. Each grain has its own setting or calibration chart.
  2. Let the sample reach room temperature if the meter requires it; very hot or cold grain gives wrong readings.
  3. Fill the meter exactly as the manufacturer instructs and take the reading. Repeat if the procedure requires two readings.
  4. Record the reading on the worksheet immediately.
  5. If the reading is near the limit or the meter seems faulty, use the reference oven method or ask your supervisor.

Sorghum kernels are small, so make sure the meter cell is filled exactly as instructed.

Determining non-compliant material

Next, weigh the working sample and separate the material that does not comply. Sort carefully on a clean tray. Put each kind in its own container and weigh it. Work out each as a percentage of the sample mass:

Percentage = mass of the material ÷ mass of the working sample × 100

Example: in a 100 g working sample you find 2.5 g of foreign matter. 2.5 ÷ 100 × 100 = 2.5%.

MaterialWhat to look for
Foreign matterStones, soil, chaff, stalk pieces, glass
Defective kernelsBroken, insect-damaged, sprouted, heat-damaged, mouldy or immature kernels
Other grainKernels of other crops such as maize or wheat
Kernels of another classHigh-tannin kernels in a low-tannin sample, or the other way round
Poisonous seedsSeeds of poisonous weeds listed in the regulations

Sprouted kernels are a big problem for malting sorghum because they no longer germinate well. Sorghum heads harvested after rain often have sprouting; look carefully.

lessons.title: Completing the grading process
lessons.html:
Completing the grading process

  1. Write every result on the worksheet: moisture and each deviation as a percentage.
  2. Compare each result with the grade table in the regulations. Start with the highest grade.
  3. The sample gets the highest grade for which all results are within the limits. If one result is over the limit for that grade, check the next grade.
  4. Check for conditions that make the sorghum non-compliant or below grade regardless of percentages, such as a musty, sour or chemical smell, live insects, or poisonous seeds above the permitted level. Report these to your supervisor straight away.
  5. Sign the worksheet or enter the result in the system. The grade goes onto the delivery ticket or certificate.
  6. Keep the reference sample, sealed and labelled, for the period the site requires, in case of a dispute.

Cleaning up

Return the sample material as instructed, clean the sieves, trays and meter, and leave the work area clean for the next sample.

Honesty

Never change a result because a farmer or driver asks you to. If someone pressures you, call your supervisor. If you made a mistake, report it and re-grade.

Key points

  • Use the current grading regulations and calibrated equipment.
  • Take a representative sample and divide it properly.
  • Set the moisture meter for sorghum and record readings straight away.
  • Percentage = mass of material ÷ sample mass × 100.
  • The grade is the highest grade for which all results comply.
